title: The era of the bands and today's young listeners
summary: They reflect on the big band era, Denver college audiences and Ted Heath.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: There were a wonderful lot of musicians.
You know, they really had good bands in those days.
Yeah, they did. The era of the bands was a wonderful thing.
Right.
It's a sad thing that it's gone into the past.
I don't know, I thought maybe they might come back again. They just might. They're trying.
Yeah, they're trying. They keep sort of lapping up to it and whatnot. The kids don't know what they're missing.
No, but they -- I found a lot of kids around here really enjoy the old bands.
Yeah, yeah. And more so all the time, don't you?
Sure. The colleges here, they love jazz.
That is wonderful.
It surprised me.
Yeah. It's -- yeah. Yeah, well, thank goodness, huh? Because that means you don't have -- for a time, every now and then, you'd think it peters right out.
Yeah.
But then -- so that's good.
And they had -- like, in England, they
had a good band, what I thought was a good band. It was -- I can't think of the name of the English band. And -- for me -- Not Ted Heath.
Ted Heath.
Yeah.
The people didn't like him in England, to me, for some reason. They say he copied.
Yeah, well, I guess he did in a way, Gus, but -
But he had a good band.
A good band, and he had good musicians, yeah.
Had a good band.
Yeah.
Had a lot of good musicians in that band.
Yeah, he did. Yeah. Yeah, well, we can be thankful to Europe for a lot of things, because it was their appreciation that increased the appreciation at home.
Sure, that's right, that's right.
